\begin{abstract}
LLM-based information extraction systems produce systematic ontology constraint violations during autoregressive generation.
On SciERC (7 relation types), 15.4\% of extracted triples violate domain/range type constraints; on DocRED (96 relation types), 18.7\%.
These violations concentrate on tightly constrained relations (e.g., \textsc{Compare}: 42.4\%, \textsc{Feature-of}: 33.5\%), while loosely constrained relations exhibit near-zero violation rates.
%
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on SciERC but only 31\% on DocRED, and is unreliable at the per-relation level---\textsc{Evaluate-for} violations \emph{increase} by 5.8 percentage points.
Prompt-level intervention thus scales poorly with ontology complexity.
%
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, which automatically compiles IE ontology schemas into two composable constraint layers for autoregressive decoding:
(1)~a \emph{grammar layer}, implemented via XGrammar, that enforces JSON structural validity and restricts entity-type and relation vocabularies to schema-defined values; and
(2)~a \emph{semantic layer} (TypeConstraintProcessor) that enforces cross-field domain/range constraints through a stateful entity registry and dynamic logit masking.
The two layers compose via bitwise AND on token-level masks, with an enabling dependency: the grammar layer guarantees well-formed output, upon which the semantic layer enforces relational type rules.
%
On SciERC, \textsc{OntoCoDec} reduces domain/range violations from 15.37\% to 0.93\% ($\downarrow$94\%) while completely eliminating entity-type and relation-vocabulary violations, with no degradation in extraction F1 ({+}0.13pp, not statistically significant).
\placeholder{DocRED results.}
However, cross-field consistency violations increase from 0.08\% to 9.9\%, a systematic side effect of per-relation independent type enforcement that represents an open challenge for future constraint composition.
\end{abstract}

% §5 Setup (compressed from Violation Landscape)
% exp_ids: mvp_phase0_violation_rate, mvp_phase0_scierc_schema,
%          mvp_phase0_violation_rate_docred, mvp_phase0_docred_schema

\label{sec:violation_landscape}

We evaluate OntoCoDec in two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 (\S\ref{sec:composability}), near-eliminating DR (DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\%) with minimal overhead; and LoRA + beam S1 (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}), achieving zero total violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation (\S\ref{sec:scierc-results}--\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) serves as a diagnostic probe; the deployment-relevant evaluation is the fine-tuned setting (R-F1 40--46\%).

\paragraph{Setup.}
We evaluate on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test sentences, 7 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) and DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} (998 dev documents,\footnote{DocRED test annotations are not publicly available; we evaluate on the development set.} 96 relations, $\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$).
RE type constraints are extracted automatically from observed type pairs in training data (neither dataset provides a formal ontology); EE constraints on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) are derived from the KAIROS ontology.
All constraints are defined from schema-level supervision, independently of the evaluation split.
The framework handles both sources without modification.
Primary model: Qwen3-8B~\cite{qwen2025qwen3}, zero-shot greedy decoding; cross-model validation in \S\ref{sec:cross-model}, composability with fine-tuning in \S\ref{sec:composability}.
We measure four violation categories: \textbf{DR} (domain/range type pair $\notin \sigma(r)$), \textbf{RV} (relation $\notin \mathcal{R}$), \textbf{ET} (entity type $\notin \mathcal{E}$), and \textbf{CF} (same entity assigned conflicting types across triples).
Baseline DR: 15.37\% (SciERC), 18.46\% (DocRED); schema-informed prompting reduces DR by 62\% on SciERC but is per-relation unreliable (Appendix~\ref{app:per-relation-landscape}).

1	% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)
2	
3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	where $\wedge$ denotes element-wise AND over the vocabulary $V$; a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the empirical enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property enforced only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation, with DR (ontologically invalid type pair) more severe than CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency).
17	
18	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
19	\label{eq:tightness}
20	We define per-relation constraint tightness $\kappa(r) = 1 - |\sigma(r)|/|\mathcal{E}|^2$ and the schema-level mean $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$.
21	Across three schemas---WikiEvents ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.029$), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$)---DR reduction ranges from 94--99\% (low $\bar{\kappa}$) to 42--90\% (high $\bar{\kappa}$); entity type confusability is a critical co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study},~\ref{app:tcr}).
22	
23	\paragraph{Greedy limitation and fallback cascade.}
24	\label{sec:greedy-limitation}
25	The semantic layer commits entity types greedily---an instance of Level~3 (non-local) constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability})---so CF violations arise when the same entity receives different types across triples; beam search mitigates this in favorable configurations (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
26	Grammar-first fallback triggers on 0.5--5.7\% of type-bearing positions under zero-shot decoding, correlating with $\bar{\kappa}$; fine-tuning virtually eliminates fallback ($\leq$\,0.11\%), transitioning the semantic layer from primary enforcer to safety net.
27	Causal tracing confirms all residual DR occurs exclusively at fallback positions (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
28	
29	\paragraph{Non-rectangularity and independent enforcement.}
30	\label{sec:rectangularity}
31	Type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED rectangular); independent enforcement is a sound over-approximation admitting 33--37\% spurious pairs; fine-tuning eliminates all residual DR (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints.
A decidability analysis yields a two-layer architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) compiles ontology constraints into grammars ensuring JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) interprets type constraints at runtime via stateful token masking over a dynamic entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
The two layers exhibit an empirical enabling dependency (Proposition~1): neither achieves full domain/range (DR) reduction alone.

Composed with LoRA fine-tuning on three 8B-class models across two RE datasets (up to 96 relation types), \textsc{OntoCoDec} achieves DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% with negligible recall cost ($<$0.5\% true-positive loss); residual cross-field violations (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\%) represent \emph{violation conversion}, resolved by beam search on SciERC (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
Zero-shot evaluation serves as a diagnostic probe, revealing dataset- and calibration-dependent DR reduction (42--99\%) and characterizing constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) as a descriptive correlate ($n{=}3$ schemas).
Preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}) and event extraction on WikiEvents (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}) confirm generalizability beyond the primary 8B evaluation.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking.
8	NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} enforces predicate-logic constraints via beam-level reranking; OntoCoDec applies constraints per-token via forward masking, avoiding beam-width dependence.
9	In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata; PICARD prunes invalid beam hypotheses post-generation, whereas OntoCoDec applies proactive token-level masking before sampling, and maintains a dynamic entity registry across multi-relation outputs rather than single-output SQL queries (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
10	
11	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
12	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie}, TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, and others~\cite{fei2022lasuie,wang2022deepstruct,lu2022uie,lou2023usm,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure or frame IE as structured generation, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.

16	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives.

19	Extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak} despite degradation in other domains~\cite{banerjee2025crane,formattax2026}.

The CF fallback variant nearly eliminates CF (9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.04\%, $-$9.86\,pp) but at the cost of a 15.9$\times$ increase in DR (0.93\%\,$\to$\,14.78\%, $+$13.85\,pp).
% exp_id: w1_cf_fallback_scierc_pilot: DR=0.1478, CF=0.0004, f_gf=0.3664
This is not a net improvement: total violations (DR+CF) rise from 10.83\% to 14.82\% ($+$3.99\,pp), so the change \emph{re-routes} violations rather than reducing them.
The mechanism is mechanical: each token position with conflicting masks must commit to one violation type; when the CF fallback forces the system to emit the entity's registered type even though it lies outside $\sigma(r)$, the resulting triple satisfies cross-entity consistency but violates domain/range.
The token-level grammar-first fallback is triggered at 36.64\% of type-bearing positions (0.46\% at first-token positions; \S\ref{sec:greedy-limitation}); this conflict is structural, not a tunable hyperparameter.

We interpret this as a fundamental tension in composable constraint systems with \emph{per-relation independent} enforcement: enforcement priority can be allocated between DR and CF but cannot independently minimize both.
Within this design, the current S1 configuration sits near the Pareto frontier of the trade-off, achieving 0.93\% DR at the cost of 9.90\% CF.
The direction of the trade-off is consistent beyond SciERC/Qwen3-8B: across all six zero-shot configurations (3 models $\times$ 2 datasets), DR and CF are descriptively inversely associated, with no setting showing both high DR and high CF simultaneously (Table~\ref{tab:cross-model}); however, $n{=}6$ is insufficient for statistical inference on this correlation.
The pattern is a structural consequence of per-relation enforcement with grammar-first fallback, not a model- or dataset-specific artifact; we select SciERC/Qwen3-8B for detailed ablation because it exhibits the highest CF (9.90\%), making the trade-off most visible.
While the inverse association holds across all configurations, the absolute trade-off magnitude may differ in settings with higher baseline CF, such as Llama DocRED (CF = 12.02\%), where the larger CF headroom could yield proportionally larger shifts under alternative fallback priorities.
The CF residual is concentrated in schema ambiguity rather than enforcement failure: 63.3\% of CF violations on SciERC involve the catch-all \textsc{Generic} type (Table~\ref{tab:cf-distribution}), which competes with every content type depending on anaphoric vs.\ referential use, a distinction the per-slot decoder cannot resolve without document-level coreference.

Two complementary paths can lower CF without re-routing it to DR.
(i)~\emph{Reduce the baseline conflict rate.} Composing OntoCoDec with LoRA fine-tuning on SciERC reduces CF by 88\% relative to the zero-shot setting (9.90\%\,$\to$\,1.18\%; Table~\ref{tab:composability}), because the fine-tuned model's per-slot type predictions agree more often with the entity registry, so the per-relation mask and the registry intersect more frequently.

The remaining 1.18\% still traces to \textsc{Generic}$\leftrightarrow$X schema ambiguity, so this path is empirically validated on one dataset and one fine-tuning method but does not generalize without further evidence.
(ii)~\emph{Replace per-relation enforcement with global entity-level type consensus during decoding.} This is outside the scope of OntoCoDec's forward-only autoregressive design and is left to future work.

1	% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)
2	
3	At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
4	The final mask is their conjunction:
5	%
6	\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
7	  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
8	\end{equation}
9	%
10	where $\wedge$ denotes element-wise AND over the vocabulary $V$; a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
11	The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the empirical enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property enforced only by the grammar layer.
12	
13	\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
14	When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
15	We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
16	Structural integrity is a hard constraint; type violations are soft errors detectable by downstream validation, with DR (ontologically invalid type pair) more severe than CF (individually valid triples with cross-triple type inconsistency).
17	
18	\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
19	\label{eq:tightness}
20	We define per-relation constraint tightness $\kappa(r) = 1 - |\sigma(r)|/|\mathcal{E}|^2$ and the schema-level mean $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$.
21	Across three schemas---WikiEvents ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.029$), SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$), DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$)---DR reduction ranges from 94--99\% (low $\bar{\kappa}$) to 42--90\% (high $\bar{\kappa}$), though this correlation is descriptive only ($n{=}3$, $p{=}0.138$); entity type confusability is a critical co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study},~\ref{app:tcr}).
22	
23	\paragraph{Greedy limitation and fallback cascade.}
24	\label{sec:greedy-limitation}
25	The semantic layer commits entity types greedily---an instance of Level~3 (non-local) constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability})---so CF violations arise when the same entity receives different types across triples; beam search mitigates this in favorable configurations (\S\ref{sec:beam-results}).
26	Grammar-first fallback triggers on 0.5--5.7\% of type-bearing positions under zero-shot decoding, correlating with $\bar{\kappa}$; fine-tuning virtually eliminates fallback ($\leq$\,0.11\%), transitioning the semantic layer from primary enforcer to safety net.
27	Causal tracing confirms all residual DR occurs exclusively at fallback positions (Appendix~\ref{app:causal-tracing}).
28	
29	\paragraph{Non-rectangularity and independent enforcement.}
30	\label{sec:rectangularity}
31	Type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED rectangular); independent enforcement is a sound over-approximation admitting 33--37\% spurious pairs; fine-tuning eliminates all residual DR (Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
32

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.
5	
6	\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
7	XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and related systems~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql,park2024grammar,jsonschemabench2025} enforce format validity via CFG-based token masking.
8	NeuroLogic Decoding~\cite{lu2021neurologic} enforces predicate-logic constraints via beam-level reranking; OntoCoDec applies constraints per-token via forward masking, avoiding beam-width dependence.
9	In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile type systems into prefix automata; PICARD prunes invalid beam hypotheses post-generation, whereas OntoCoDec applies proactive token-level masking before sampling, and maintains a dynamic entity registry across multi-relation outputs rather than single-output SQL queries (\S\ref{sec:composition}).
10	
11	\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
12	GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, GenIE~\cite{josifoski2022genie}, TANL~\cite{paolini2021tanl}, REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, and others~\cite{fei2022lasuie,wang2022deepstruct,lu2022uie,lou2023usm,zhou2024universalner} encode ontology structure or frame IE as structured generation, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
13	GoLLIE and KnowCoder embed schema knowledge via code-style prompts, representing training-time schema internalization without runtime enforcement; GoLLIE-7B eliminates DR via its dataclass format but at severe coverage cost (E-F1${=}$9.17, R-F1${=}$0.0, 46\% empty output), while OntoCoDec with LoRA achieves R-F1${=}$45.47 at DR${=}$0.09\%, surpassing KnowCoder-7B (supervised R-F1${=}$40.0)~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024}.
14	
15	\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
16	\citet{roth_yih_2004} and \citet{riedel2010modeling} formulated hard type constraints via ILP; post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025} detects violations after generation but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives.
17	EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} uses ASP; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} backtracks on violations---OntoCoDec uses forward-only masking at $O(|V|)$ per step, avoiding backtracking latency.
18	Grammar-only enforcement (GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd}, BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025}) achieves only 3\% DR reduction (\S\ref{sec:constrained-baselines}); DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} explores draft-conditioned constrained decoding.
19	Extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak} despite degradation in other domains~\cite{banerjee2025crane,formattax2026}.
20

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity necessarily carries a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 0.5--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with schema restrictiveness (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
At competitive quality (R-F1 40--46\%), even 1--2\% residual violations compound across thousands of documents into systematic knowledge graph corruption, making reliable constraint enforcement necessary.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} ensures syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering improves precision but discards up to 48\% of predictions including true positives (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}); at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it becomes impractical.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} internalize schema knowledge but provide only soft guidance without runtime enforcement; no method provides both semantic awareness and hard constraint enforcement.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that translates IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} compiles ontology constraints into context-free grammars (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} interprets type constraints at runtime via dynamic logit masking over an entity registry, with an \emph{empirical enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and is applicable to autoregressive LMs with logits access; we validate on three English datasets (up to 96 relation types), three 8B-class models across three tokenizer families, with preliminary 70B-class validation (\S\ref{sec:70b-results}).
LoRA + greedy S1 achieves near-complete DR elimination: DR\,$\leq$\,0.09\% at R-F1 43--46\% ($\pm$0.8\,pp, $+$10\% latency); beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violation types on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
DR enforcement converts ontologically invalid violations to individually valid but type-inconsistent ones (CF\,$\leq$\,1.4\% fine-tuned; \S\ref{sec:scierc-results}); zero-shot evaluation reveals DR drops 42--99\% across models and datasets, with 76--99\% on SciERC, but total violations (DR+CF) decrease by $\sim$31\%, reflecting conversion that fine-tuning resolves (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}).

We make a systematic engineering contribution with theoretical grounding:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A two-layer constrained decoding framework: we formalize a well-known intuition that cross-field type constraints require runtime state beyond context-free expressiveness (Proposition~1), yielding pair-based sequential enforcement at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from IE ontologies, validated on schemas of varying restrictiveness with up to 96 relation types.
